beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing an agent is not one thing. You pick between context, a skill, an output or an interface, and that choice is strategy.

beats.trigger: Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.
beats.got: I already have this example. It's the learning portal we bought two years ago.

beats.trigger: **Find** the absorption bottleneck and draft the technical plan and the people plan together
beats.got: There is a people plan next to the technical plan. That is the part I came for.

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to have: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack?
beats.got: I think I get the options, but I haven't built a memory folder or a skill, so I can't judge them yet.

beats.trigger: Start with the teammate's work, not with *"what should I share with my teammate?"*
beats.got: Start from what the other person is trying to get done, not from what I built. That is how I'd run any HR project.

beats.trigger: If the agent ranges too wide, interrupt with *"tell me what you've found so far, narrow to the files that bear on this teammate, then continue."*
beats.got: The agent reads my files and writes a job description for a colleague. I'm not sure what is in my working set, and nobody has explained jtbd.md.

beats.trigger: *"Share the whole agent"* is not on the list.
beats.got: There are four ways to share. The reason has to be the colleague's outcome, not that we happen to have the platform.

beats.trigger: finds what would stop that candidate from being absorbed and turns it into a technical plan plus a people plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Two plans, one obstacle that decides it.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one obstacle that keeps several others hard, not the first technical complaint. It's a root cause, and I know that from change work.

beats.trigger: `module-7/people-plan.md` should name who owns, governs, operates, judges, and propagates it.
beats.got: The people plan has to name an owner, a governor, an operator, a judge and someone who spreads it. This is the first time AI training has asked who owns it after I leave the room. I could show this to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses until someone tests them.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Ask what would have to be true for them to switch. 'Fire their current hire' is a bit odd when the hire is a spreadsheet, but I follow the idea.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: Imagine it failed and write three stories of why. It is a pre-mortem, which I like. It ends in one person, one question and one test.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Picking by outcome is design. Picking by what fits the platform is shopping.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute. Absorption happens in other people's weeks, at their pace, for their reasons.
beats.got: A licence rollout counts access. Whether people use the tool is a different number, and the two get reported as one.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: Even a good agent-built analysis stalled because the leaders didn't own it and urgency faded. Companies run on trust between people, and that is what I see in my leadership team too.

beats.trigger: The fourth does not copy at all, which is why the product being sold as a shared agent is always three of the four parts, with the fourth still sitting with whoever built it.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy. Accountability does not. A named person has to answer for what the agent does, and that is a people question.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each sharing strategy demands something different from the receiver: trust, fit, habit, or someone to keep it running.

beats.trigger: Not *how do I get them to adopt this?* but *what would have to be true for them to switch?*
beats.got: Ask what has to be true for them, not how to push adoption. The answers are small: it shows up where they already look, and someone they trust has used it first.

beats.trigger: You cannot schedule absorption from your side.
beats.got: Start with one person and one conversation before building more. That is realistic.

beats.trigger: Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention?
beats.got: Different people need different forms of sharing. I'd sort my HR partners that way.

beats.trigger: Write the technical plan and the people plan together.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: I bring back what the person said, not my plan.

beats.trigger: ## Next
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Before I share anything, I ask one colleague how they do the job today. I don't start from what I built.
An agent copies as context, a skill, an output or an interface. The accountable person does not copy, so every plan needs a named owner next to the technical part.
Access is not absorption. When I report rollouts to leadership I will ask how many people actually use the tool, not how many have a licence.

monday.move: Ask one of my HR business partners how they prepare the weekly people-metrics summary today and what would make them trust a draft from an agent. I build nothing yet.
monday.stop_condition: If they say they would never use it, or if it needs employee data. Then I ask the DPO and the works council first and don't build anything.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked either yet.

misconception.why: I still expect the headcount question in the leadership meeting. But the module showed me that even a working agent stalls on trust, ownership and urgency. So 'which roles go' is the wrong first question, and the module never gave me a better answer to bring to leadership.

one_line: It is less about agents than about why people don't pick up what you hand them. There's a good story on how a good analysis died in a leadership meeting, but I'd want a better answer on headcount.
